title: Can and can't
intro: Turkmen has no single word for **can**. You join the verb to *bilmek*, **to know**, with the linking form `-(Y)p`: *ýüzüp bilýärin*, I can swim, literally **swimming, I know**. This unit builds that form, makes it negative (*gelip bilmeýärin*, *gelip bilmerin*, *gelip bilmedim*), shows how to ask for permission and talk about what is possible (*Girsem bolýarmy?*, *Bu ýerde oturyp bolýar*, *mümkin*), and adds the words for **nobody**, **nothing** and **never**, which need a negative verb.

blocks.text: First, the linking form of the verb, the converb in `-(Y)p`. After a consonant, add *-yp* or *-ip*: *gel-* → *gelip*, *al-* → *alyp*. After a rounded vowel in a one-syllable stem it is *-up* or *-üp*, by the rounding rule of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *gör-* → *görüp*, *bol-* → *bolup*, *ýüz-* → *ýüzüp*. After a vowel, just *-p*: *oka-* → *okap*, and a final *e* becomes *ä*: *işle-* → *işläp*, *gürle-* → *gürläp*.

The *t*-verbs that become *d* before a vowel do it here too: *gidip*, *edip*, *aýdyp*, *kömek edip*. The converb itself never changes: no tense, no person. Everything else goes on *bilmek*, in any tense you know: *ýüzüp bilýärin*, I can swim; *ýüzüp bilerin*, I'll be able to swim; *ýüzüp bildim*, I could swim, I managed to swim.

blocks.title: Knowing and being able
blocks.text: On its own, *bilmek* means **to know**: *Men türkmençe bilýärin*, I know Turkmen. With a converb it means **can**: *Men türkmençe gürläp bilýärin*, I can speak Turkmen. Both are common, and in practice they say much the same.

blocks.title: Two words, one ending
blocks.text: The converb and *bilmek* are written apart: *ýüzüp bilýärin*, not `ýüzüpbilýärin`. Only *bilmek* takes endings: not `ýüzýärin bilýärin`, and not `ýüzmek bilýärin`.

For **can't**, make *bilmek* negative and leave the converb as it is. Each tense of *bilmek* gives its own shade: *gelip bilmeýärin*, I can't come (now, these days); *gelip bilmerin*, I won't be able to come, I can't come (a refusal or a prediction); *gelip bilmedim*, I couldn't come.

blocks.text: **Questions** put `-mY` on *bilmek*, as on any verb: *Ýüzüp bilýärsiňmi?*, can you swim? *Gelip bildiňmi?*, were you able to come? The general present makes a polite request: *Kömek edip bilersiňizmi?*, could you help? *Haýal gürläp bilersiňizmi?*, could you speak slowly?

blocks.title: The negative goes on bilmek
blocks.text: Not `gelmän bilýärin` or `gelmeýip bilýärin`: the converb has no negative here. **I can't come** is *gelip bilmeýärin*, with *-me-* in *bilmek*.
`-(Y)p bilmek` covers what you are able to do and what you know how to do. For what is **allowed** or **possible**, Turkmen has three other tools.

**`-(Y)p bolýar`: one can.** The converb with *bolýar* (from *bolmak*), with no person: *Bu ýerde oturyp bolýar*, you can sit here, it's all right to sit here. The negative is *bolmaýar*: *Bu ýerde çilim çekip bolmaýar*, you can't smoke here. As a question it asks for permission: *Içeri girip bolýarmy?*, can we go in? may I go in?

**Asking politely.** *Girsem bolýarmy?* (May I come in?) and *Sorasam bolýarmy?* (May I ask?) are the everyday ways to ask for permission. Their *-sem* is the conditional, which comes in [B1 unit 9](b1-u09); for now, learn them as set phrases. The usual answers: *Hawa, bolýar* (yes, that's fine) or *Ýok, bolmaýar* (no, it isn't allowed).

**mümkin: possible.** *Bu mümkin*, that's possible; *Bu mümkin däl*, that's impossible; *Mümkinmi?*, may I? is it possible? And `-(Y)p biler`, the general present of *bilmek*, says what **may** happen: *Ol gelip biler*, he may come; *Ertir ýagyş ýagyp biler*, it may rain tomorrow.

items.en: May I come in? — Yes, of course.
I asked my father for permission.

blocks.title: Permission, the word
blocks.text: *rugsat* is **permission**: *rugsat soramak*, to ask for permission (from someone, with `-dAn`); *rugsat bermek*, to give it (to someone, with the dative): *Kakam maňa rugsat berdi*, my father let me.

blocks.title: Can, may, might
blocks.text: English **can** covers ability (**I can swim**), permission (**can I come in?**) and possibility (**it can happen**). Turkmen tends to split them: *ýüzüp bilýärin* for ability, *girip bolýarmy?* or *Girsem bolýarmy?* for permission, *bolup biler* or *mümkin* for possibility.

In [A1 unit 5](a1-u05) you met *hiç kim* and *hiç zat* with *ýok*: *Öýde hiç kim ýok*. With a verb, these words need the verb in the **negative** too. English says **nobody came**; Turkmen says, in effect, **nobody didn't come**: *Hiç kim gelmedi*.

items.en: I didn't see anything. I saw nothing.
I have no money at all.

blocks.text: The positive words are simpler. *biri* is **someone**: *Gapyda biri bar*, there's someone at the door. *bir zat* is **something**, *bir ýerde* **somewhere**. *hemme* is **everyone** or **everything** (*hemmeler* for people, *hemme zat* for things), and *her kim* is **everyone, anyone**: *Her kim gelip biler*, anyone can come.
**Short answers** can be the *hiç* word alone: *Kim geldi? — Hiç kim.* (Who came? — Nobody.) *Näme gördüň? — Hiç zat.* (What did you see? — Nothing.)

blocks.title: Don't forget the negative
blocks.text: `Hiç kim geldi` and `Men hiç zat gördüm` are wrong: with *hiç*, the verb is negative: *Hiç kim gelmedi*, *Men hiç zat görmedim*. In a sentence with *bar* or *ýok*, use *ýok*: *Hiç zat ýok*, not `Hiç zat bar`.

summary: The converb is stem + `-(Y)p`: *gelip, alyp, görüp, okap, işläp, gidip*. It never changes.
**Can** is converb + *bilmek* in any tense: *ýüzüp bilýärin* (I can swim), *gelip bilerin* (I'll be able to come), *gelip bildim* (I could come).
**Can't** makes *bilmek* negative: *bilmeýärin*, *bilmerin*, *bilmedim*. A polite request: *Kömek edip bilersiňizmi?*
Permission and possibility: *oturyp bolýar* (you can sit), *Girsem bolýarmy?* (may I come in?), *mümkin* (possible), *gelip biler* (he may come).
*hiç kim, hiç zat, hiç ýerde, hiç haçan* need a negative verb: *Hiç kim gelmedi*.
